articles.title: Philippines Snubs China at ASEAN Defense Meeting Amid South China Sea Tensions - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Philippines Snubs China at ASEAN Defense Meeting Amid South China Sea Tensions  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Lapu-Lapu City, Philippines — Defense leaders from across the Indo-Pacific gathered in Cebu this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) premier defense diplomacy events, but the proceedings were overshadowed by a deliberate diplomatic snub directed at Beijing and escalating maritime confrontations in the South China Sea.
The 20th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) and the 13th ADMM-Plus, held on October 28 and 29, served as a critical platform for regional security dialogue. However, the host nation, the Philippines, utilized its 2026 ASEAN Chairmanship to firmly align the bloc’s security architecture with international maritime law, directly challenging China’s expansive territorial claims.
A Calculated Diplomatic Distance
The most visible manifestation of the strained relations occurred during the ADMM-Plus plenary sessions, which include eight key dialogue partners such as the United States, Japan, and Australia. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro notably excluded Chinese representatives from key bilateral and minilateral security consultations on the sidelines of the summit.
Diplomatic sources in Cebu confirmed that Manila deliberately bypassed standard courtesy engagements with the Chinese delegation, a move interpreted as a direct response to recent aggressive maneuvers by Chinese coast guard vessels against Philippine resupply missions in the disputed Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal. The snub signals a hardening of Manila’s posture, shifting away from the traditional ASEAN consensus of quiet diplomacy toward a more confrontational, rules-based approach to regional security.
South China Sea Dominates the Agenda
While the official communiqué emphasized ASEAN unity and non-traditional security threats like disaster response and cyber defense, the closed-door sessions were dominated by the deteriorating situation in the West Philippine Sea. Defense ministers from Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia reportedly expressed strong support for the Philippines’ insistence on upholding the 2016 arbitral ruling, which invalidated China’s nine-dash line claim.
The presence of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other Plus partners underscored the internationalization of the dispute. The United States reiterated its ironclad commitments under the Mutual Defense Treaty, warning that any armed attack on Philippine public vessels in the South China Sea would trigger a US response. This explicit security guarantee has emboldened Manila to take a harder line within ASEAN forums, frustrating Chinese diplomats who have long sought to keep the dispute strictly bilateral and isolated from multilateral security architectures.
Regional Threats and Strategic Realignment
Beyond the maritime disputes, the Cebu meetings addressed a broader spectrum of regional threats, including the proliferation of advanced military technologies and the deepening strategic partnership between Beijing and Moscow. ASEAN members expressed concern over the potential deployment of dual-use technologies and the militarization of artificial islands, which they argue destabilizes the regional balance of power.
The ADMM-Plus also focused on enhancing interoperability among partner nations for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR), a relatively neutral area where cooperation with China is still maintained. However, the underlying strategic divergence was palpable. While China advocated for an "Asian security model" led by regional powers without external interference, the Philippines and its Western partners pushed for an "open, inclusive, and rules-based" architecture that explicitly welcomes the continued presence of external powers to balance regional hegemony.
As the summit concluded, the message from Cebu was unequivocal. The Philippines, leveraging its chairmanship, has successfully shifted the center of gravity within ASEAN’s defense establishment. By openly snubbing Beijing and deepening military integration with the US and its allies, Manila is betting that collective deterrence and international legal frameworks offer a more viable path to securing its sovereign rights than the traditional ASEAN doctrine of non-interference and consensus-driven accommodation.
The implications of the Cebu meetings extend far beyond the immediate diplomatic theater. For smaller ASEAN states, the Philippine strategy presents both an opportunity and a risk. While it provides a stronger collective voice against coercion, it also raises the specter of forcing member states to choose sides in an intensifying great-power rivalry. Indonesia and Singapore, traditionally the architects of ASEAN’s hedging strategy, spent much of the summit attempting to bridge the gap between Manila’s assertiveness and the desire of other members to maintain stable economic ties with Beijing.
Ultimately, the 2026 ADMM cycle will be remembered as the moment the Philippines successfully weaponized its ASEAN chairmanship to redraw the region's security fault lines, ensuring that the South China Sea remains the defining geopolitical flashpoint of the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: Latest IMF Forecast: Vietnam's GDP Per Capita to Surpass Indonesia's for First Time in 2026, Rising to Fifth in ASEAN - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Latest IMF Forecast: Vietnam's GDP Per Capita to Surpass Indonesia's for First Time in 2026, Rising to Fifth in ASEAN  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) latest forecast shows that Vietnam's nominal GDP per capita will reach $5,259 in 2026, up 8.9% from the previous year, surpassing Indonesia's $5,153 for the first time. This turning point means Vietnam will rise to fifth place among ASEAN member states in GDP per capita, trailing only Thailand.
Vietnam's population is currently about 100 million, while Indonesia's is about 290 million—nearly a threefold difference—making this crossover in the per-capita indicator particularly noteworthy. GDP per capita is calculated by dividing total GDP by population; nominal values are measured at current prices without inflation adjustment and are also affected by exchange-rate fluctuations when converted into dollars.
Vietnam's growth momentum stems mainly from its gradual emergence as a high-tech manufacturing base alternative to China. As supply chains for electronic components and semiconductors accelerate their relocation, international industry giants such as Taiwan's Hon Hai Group (2317.TW) and South Korea's Samsung Electronics are continuing to expand production in Vietnam, driving large-scale exports of smartphones and other electronic products.
Export and foreign investment data reflect this trend. In the first nine months of this year, Vietnam's exports reached $434.3 billion, up 25% year-on-year; foreign direct investment (FDI) reached $21.1 billion, up 12% year-on-year. Registered capital, a leading indicator of investment, surged 76% to $50.3 billion, showing that foreign investors' long-term commitment to Vietnam has not cooled.
Public infrastructure is another core engine. Vietnam plans to invest about VND 1,000 trillion (approximately $38.8 billion) in 2026 to advance nationwide roads, airports and other infrastructure. Mai Fujita, a senior researcher at Japan's Institute of Developing Economies, noted: "The Vietnamese government's active public investment is supporting economic growth."
On growth, Vietnam's government has set a target of at least 10% economic growth in 2026, while the IMF's latest report forecasts 8.4% growth for Vietnam in 2026, the highest in Southeast Asia. By comparison, Indonesia's growth remains around 5%, with a forecast of 5.1% for 2026.
Although Indonesia has worked hard to attract foreign investment in industries such as electric vehicles, those funds have not effectively translated into sufficient jobs and real income growth, and a weaker rupiah has curbed the growth of its dollar-denominated nominal GDP per capita.
Looking ahead, Vietnam has set a target of raising GDP per capita to $8,500 by 2030, equivalent to Thailand's current level. Fujita believes that beyond short-term infrastructure investment to stimulate growth, Vietnam also needs to "strive for long-term growth, such as developing human resources and technology."
For investors, the forecast highlights that ASEAN's manufacturing landscape is being reshaped. Vietnam is catching up rapidly with an export-oriented, foreign-investment-driven model, while Indonesia faces the challenge of turning foreign investment into real wage growth. The golden crossover in the two countries' per-capita income will also become an important indicator for regional supply-chain positioning and capital flows.
Note: GDP per capita figures are nominal values, calculated at current prices without inflation adjustment, and are affected by exchange-rate movements when converted into dollars.

articles.title: The Ministry of Industry and Trade works with electronics businesses on the import and export situation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Ministry of Industry and Trade works with electronics businesses on the import and export situation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 30th, in Hanoi, the Ministry of Industry and Trade held a meeting with major electronics businesses to assess the production and import-export situation, clarify the causes of the trade deficit, and discuss the industry's development prospects in the coming period.
Electronics exports surged, but the trade deficit remained large.
In his opening remarks, Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Luong Hoang Thai acknowledged and highly appreciated the efforts of the electronics business community, while emphasizing the role of this industry in Vietnam's export activities.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
According to information from the Import-Export Department of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, it is estimated that Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025, officially surpassing the US$1 trillion mark. In October alone, import and export turnover is estimated at US$122.2 billion, an increase of 47.6% compared to the same period last year.
Notably, exports continued to grow strongly, with estimated turnover reaching $499 billion in the first 10 months, an increase of 27.4%, creating positive momentum to achieve and surpass the export growth target of 15-16% for the whole year of 2026.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
In the import-export structure, the electronics industry continues to affirm its position as one of the leading industries, making a significant contribution to the country's export turnover.
According to data from the Customs Department, Ministry of Finance , as of October 15, 2026, the cumulative export value of the two product groups, computers, electronic products and components; and telephones of all types and components, reached US$189.65 billion, accounting for approximately 40% of the country's total export value.
Specifically, the group of computers, electronic products, and components reached $135.3 billion, a 65% increase compared to the same period in 2025. According to assessments presented at the meeting, the increasing demand for artificial intelligence ( AI ) equipment and data centers globally is one of the factors driving the export growth of this product group.

However, despite positive export results, the trade balance of the electronics industry is raising concerns. Specifically, the total import value of the two major electronics product groups reached $209.7 billion. Of this, imports of computers, electronic products, and components reached approximately $201 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of $65.69 billion for this group.
Although the group of telephones and components recorded a trade surplus of over $45.67 billion, the overall trade balance of the two product groups still showed a deficit of approximately $20 billion.
Notably, after 10 consecutive years of maintaining a trade surplus, Vietnam's trade balance shifted to a deficit in 2026. This development necessitates a more thorough assessment of the import-export structure, especially for the electronics industry – a sector with high export value but currently recording a significant deficit.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Finding solutions to the electronics industry's trade deficit problem.
At the meeting, Mr. Tran Thanh Hai, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), presented an overview of the production, import-export situation and development prospects of Vietnam's electronics industry.
“ Vietnam has become one of the important electronics manufacturing locations in the global supply chain, with the presence of many large corporations such as Samsung , LG, Intel, Foxconn, and Canon,” Mr. Tran Thanh Hai emphasized.
However, the production structure of the electronics industry remains clearly differentiated. While foreign-invested enterprises (FDI) play a dominant role in manufacturing, assembly, and export, domestic enterprises mainly participate in component production, supporting industries, and providing technical services.
Notably, one of the reasons for the trade deficit is the sharp increase in demand for imported raw materials and components for production. Some types of chips have seen price increases of 300-500%, causing a significant increase in import value even when import volume has not increased proportionally.
In addition, businesses are increasing their accumulation and stockpiling of raw materials and components to support production plans, while simultaneously expanding factory scale, production lines, and exports. This leads to a demand for importing machinery, equipment, and input materials.
Another issue highlighted is that electronics manufacturing in Vietnam remains heavily reliant on imported components and raw materials, while the localization rate and added value generated domestically are limited.
You may also like
Based on the above situation, the Import-Export Department has outlined several development directions for the electronics industry, focusing on attracting investment in key electronics sectors, developing the semiconductor industry, research and development (R&D), enhancing the capacity of supporting industries, and strengthening linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises.
This also includes the need to diversify markets and supply sources, improve the quality of human resources and logistics capabilities, aiming to transform Vietnam from a manufacturing and assembly center into a higher-value link in the global electronics supply chain.
Speaking at the meeting, Deputy Minister Luong Hoang Thai requested that businesses and delegates focus on analyzing the current state of development in the electronics industry, clarifying the causes of the trade deficit, and assessing the prospects for production, import, and export in the coming period. In a spirit of frankness, cooperation, and responsibility, the discussions delved into practical issues, contributing to a more accurate assessment and forecast of the import situation as well as the development prospects of Vietnam's electronics industry.
According to data from the Customs Department, as of October 15, 2026, the export value of two product groups – computers, electronic products and components; and telephones and components – reached US$189.65 billion, accounting for approximately 40% of the country's total export value. However, the import value of these two product groups amounted to US$209.7 billion, corresponding to a trade deficit of approximately US$20 billion.

China has accused the Philippines of setting up “numerous obstacles” to attending a meeting with defence ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and of violating “basic diplomatic protocols”.
“The Philippines has allowed certain politicians to act recklessly and abuse public power for personal agendas, erecting numerous obstacles to hinder China’s participation,” Senior Colonel Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesman for the defence ministry, said on Thursday.
